A.explanation: This shows steep gradient then shallow then steep again, which would mean large then small then large acceleration. The $F$-$t$ triangle does not do this.

B.explanation: Gradient of $v$-$t$ equals acceleration, which follows the triangular $F$. Gradient starts at zero, is steepest at peak $F$, then falls to zero leaving constant $v$.

C.explanation: A horizontal then vertical drop in $v$ would need infinite acceleration. The force on the ball is finite and varies smoothly as a triangle.

D.explanation: This shows $v$ suddenly reversing to negative values. The force is always in the forward direction, so $v$ must keep increasing while $F$ acts.

hints: Notice the $F$-$t$ graph is a triangle starting at zero, rising to a peak and falling back to zero at contact time.
Recall that for the ball $F = ma$, so the gradient of the $v$-$t$ graph must rise and fall in the same way as $F$.
Check which $v$-$t$ shape starts flat, gets steepest when $F$ is largest, then levels flat again once $F$ is zero.
walkthrough: The ball starts from rest with $v=0$ at $t=0$. While in contact, the club exerts the triangular force $F$ shown.
Use $F = ma$, so $a = F/m$. Acceleration is proportional to $F$, so $a$-$t$ is also a triangle starting at zero, peaking, then returning to zero.
On a $v$-$t$ graph, gradient $= a = dv/dt$. So the $v$-$t$ gradient must start at zero, increase to a maximum, then decrease back to zero.
That means $v$ increases slowly at first, then more rapidly near peak force, then more slowly again - an S-shaped rise.
After $F$ returns to zero, $a = 0$, so gradient is zero and $v$ stays constant at its final take-off value.
Only graph B shows this flat-steep-flat gradient change to a constant velocity. This is option B
